summary:
Visa and border treatment of transgender visitors is set out in the official WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 safety and travel guidance: visa requirements depend on nationality alone, with gender identity playing no part in the application, and a passport carrying a gender marker that differs from the marker assigned at birth or an 'X' marker is accepted provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited under Dutch law, and since 1 July 2025 a discriminatory motive is written into criminal law as a ground for increasing penalties, alongside expanded rights for victims and protection of victim data. Same-sex marriage is legal, non-binary people are legally recognised, conversion therapy is banned and access to sex-segregated facilities is protected, so a trans traveller's relationship status raises no entry or registration issue.

Official victimisation figures published by the Dutch government show that more than 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, rising to 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people. The 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism recorded a sharp rise in incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence, and in 2022 one third of discrimination reports reaching the police concerned sexual orientation.

Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is climbing in measurable terms. Police figures relayed by Transgender Netwerk record 4,800 reports concerning LGBTQIA+ people last year, 7.5% above 2024 and 81% above the 2,654 recorded in 2022. Reports specifically about transgender people rose 51% within a single year, from 264 to 399, while COC describes the trend as extremely worrying and notes that only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination followed last year's reports.

Pride-period conditions carry their own documented incident load. During the opening of WorldPride Amsterdam in July 2026, more than 70 people filed discrimination reports through the RITA platform, most of them festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and participants in the Pride Walk; RITA states that these reports represent only a fraction of the total. Mayor Halsema told the city council that discrimination and violent incidents will be handled as a priority during World Pride, with police, enforcers and organisers agreed to act quickly, and recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators leaving the scene before intervention.

Practical reporting infrastructure is extensive for the event. Amsterdam broadened its Safer Spaces reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence across the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. The capital remains among the safer large European cities for ordinary street crime, and the combination of legal protection, priority police response and multiple physical reporting channels gives a trans visitor clear routes to assistance.
tangentialFactors:
The Netherlands sits within a broad European legal framework that treats gender identity as a protected ground: discrimination in employment and housing on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, homosexuality is legal, and Equaldex records high public support for LGBT openness, with the country ranked second of 121 regions as a good place for LGBT people.

The reporting surge needs reading against the recording machinery behind it. Dutch legislation contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination (ECAD-P), and the 2022 finding that a third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation reflects that channel rather than a separate hate-crime register.

Equaldex separately states that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only, which sits alongside the national criminal-law mechanism making any discriminatory motive an aggravating factor from 1 July 2025. The gap between rising report volumes and the six convictions recorded for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination last year indicates that formal outcomes remain rare even as reporting becomes more common.

Document rules a trans traveller may inspect before travel remain restrictive for residents: legal gender change still requires a letter from a medical expert rather than self-declaration, the 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months, and the self-ID Transgender Act was withdrawn in July 2025. These constraints affect resident documentation, not the entry rules applied to visitors carrying an officially issued passport with an amended or 'X' marker.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in the Netherlands continues to depend on a medical expert's letter, a standard that falls short of self-determination. The 'X' gender marker can only be obtained through a court petition that takes between three and nine months, and the Transgender Act providing self-identification was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation has been offered to people who were sterilised under earlier legal requirements.

The placement of transgender detainees has no governing statute. NJCM's criminal-law working group advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection on 21 February 2024 that no law, regulation or official policy governs where transgender detainees are held; the Penitentiary Principles Act separates only male and female detainees. The Prison Service (DJI) confirmed that placement follows the gender designation recorded in the municipal population register (BRP) together with case-by-case factors such as gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background and physical or mental health, while DIZ was drafting guidelines that remained unpublished.

Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an Extra Care Facility (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they are held alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing at arrival before transfer to an EZV, and a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution and later transferred to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, where she reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation. Sentencing rulings by the Limburg court (17 October 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) and the Hague appeals court (29 June 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108) treated placement on a wing that does not match the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM has asked the minister to create rules aligned with CPT standards that place transgender detainees according to gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether hate-crime law covers gender identity is unresolved across sources: Equaldex records hate-crime protections as covering sexual orientation only, while the government's own July 2025 measures make any discriminatory motive a ground for increased penalties in criminal cases. The scope of the aggravating-factor rule as applied to gender identity is not specified in the available material.

RITA has stated that the 70-plus discrimination reports filed at the opening of WorldPride 2026 are only a fraction of the total, so no reliable count of incidents during the event exists. Recent Pride baselines of 25 to 45 reports are themselves reported figures rather than measures of underlying incidence.

Official Dutch victimisation statistics for transgender people (17% experiencing physical or sexual violence) and the report trend (transgender-specific reports up 51% in a year) come from different collection systems and cannot be directly compared. The discrepancy between 4,800 reports and six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination last year is unexplained in the source material.

NJCM records that no official figures exist on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and that the placement guidelines under drafting by DIZ were unpublished as of February 2024. The current status of those guidelines and of the minister's response to the advice is not documented in the available inventory.
